extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy (aesthetics) and readers interested in Kantian theory of taste
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and principles for making and evaluating judgements of taste (what counts as beauty), emphasizing their a priori, subjective, and communicable character and the mental conditions (imagination, understanding) that ground aesthetic judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Autonomy of taste
rubrics_metrics.description: The subject must judge by himself, without needing to consult or accommodate the judgements of others; the judgement should be pronounced a priori and not be a mere imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a young poet should not abandon his own conviction of beauty merely because the public or friends disagree; to follow others in order to gain applause is heteronomy (an anti-pattern). Autonomy means one may later revise taste through exercise, but not because others' immediate agreement compels it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic judgement not based on concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: A judgement of taste is not determinable by concepts and is generally not cognitive; it does not subsume the representation under a concept of the object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because it is not grounded in concepts, it cannot be expressed as an objective, conceptual rule. Attempts to treat beauty as a conceptual predicate (as in logical judgements) miss the nature of aesthetic judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: A priori claim of universal validity despite subjectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the judgement of taste is subjectively grounded (a feeling), it claims the assent of all subjects as if it were an a priori, universally valid judgement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The judgement is singular (e.g. 'this tulip is beautiful') yet asserts that others ought to share the same feeling; this is a defining paradoxical feature of taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not determinable by empirical or a priori proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: No empirical grounds (others' praise) nor a priori rules/proofs can legitimately determine or force a judgement about beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics' rules or the unanimous praise of others cannot compel one's inner agreement; one may reinterpret the rules as false or inapplicable rather than change one's immediate aesthetic judgement. Anti-pattern: treating critic citations or rule-lists as conclusive proof of beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disinterestedness of aesthetic pleasure (no determining interest)
rubrics_metrics.description: The judgement of taste must have no interest as its determining ground; the pleasure involved should be 'disinterested' rather than motivated by desire, utility, or social advantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish empirical interest (sociability, vanity), intellectual/moral interest, and pure aesthetical pleasure. Judging something beautiful because it benefits one, enhances status, or gratifies senses (enjoyment) is an anti-pattern; only when pleasure is bound up with mere reflection (not with a purpose or desire) is it pure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicability of the feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Taste is the faculty of judging a priori the universal communicability of the feeling bound up with a given representation, i.e. whether the feeling can be communicated to others without mediation by concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One presumes the subjective conditions of judgement to be common to all and imputes to everyone the same subjective purposiveness that one experiences oneself. This is not a claim about actual agreement but about the appropriateness of expecting communicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjective purposiveness (feeling of purposiveness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty is constituted by a feeling that the representation exhibits subjective purposiveness for the judging faculties — a purposiveness of the form of the representation for the free play of cognitive faculties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The determining ground for aesthetic judgement is the felt purposiveness of the representation (how it invites harmonious cognitive play), not any objective purpose or concept. Critics may use examples to illustrate this purposiveness, but cannot reduce it to a formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmony of Imagination and Understanding (free play)
rubrics_metrics.description: The judgement of taste rests on the harmonious interplay in imagination (its freedom in schematising) and the understanding (its conformity to law); the representation should put these faculties into regular, pleasurable play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good aesthetic object is one whose form allows imagination to be free while being receptive to the normative activity of understanding. Criterion focuses on formal relations, not sensory matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensus communis and reflective maxims
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a communal standpoint (sensus communis) in reflection: compare one's judgement with the possible judgements of others, abstract from private conditions, and apply three maxims — think for oneself; put oneself in the place of every other; and think consistently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These maxims help avoid prejudice and heteronomy: (1) think unprejudicedly, (2) enlarge thought by imagining others' perspectives, (3) maintain consecutive (consistent) thought. Anti-patterns: prejudice, passive reliance on authorities, superstition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Following exemplary models without imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples and classical models are necessary to sharpen taste, but their proper influence is 'following' (learning the sources and method), not mechanical imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exemplary authors guide others toward developing their own principles and methods; they should not be treated as laws that make successors mere imitators. Useful as training and orientation, not as determinative rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish kinds of pleasure: beauty vs enjoyment vs moral/sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasures differ: enjoyment (sensory), moral pleasure (connected to concepts and duty), pleasure in the sublime (linked to rational contemplation), and pleasure in the beautiful (mere reflection). The pleasure of the beautiful is distinct and must not be conflated with mere sensory charm or with interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not judge something beautiful merely because it gratifies the senses or because it serves social/moral ends. Natural beauty can arouse an immediate intellectual interest (valuing its presence for itself); artificial imitations may lose that immediate interest when revealed. Anti-pattern: equating charm or utility with genuine beauty.
